```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(multiScaleR)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

# Choose the prediction question first

Cross-validation (CV) assesses predictions for observations excluded from model
fitting. For scale-of-effect models, the exclusion must apply to ecological
scales and learned predictor transformations as well as regression coefficients.
Fitting scales on the full data before dividing rows into folds would use
information from the assessment data.

The fold design determines the prediction question. Holding out rows at random
can assess new observations near the sampled locations. Holding out whole
animals or sites assesses transfer to excluded sampling groups. Spatial blocks
and training buffers assess predictions across a chosen geographic separation.
None of these designs automatically establishes independence or calibration.
Choose groups, block size, buffer, candidate models and scoring rules before
examining the assessment outcomes.

| Function | Use |
|:--|:--|
| `grouped_cv_folds()` | Keep whole sampling groups in one assessment fold |
| `spatial_cv_folds()` | Keep whole projected grid blocks, optionally joined by groups |
| `cross_validate()` | Refit spatial scales and GLM coefficients within each fold |
| `cross_validate_glm()` | Fit ordinary GLM reference or null models within each fold |
| `cv_tab()` | Compare pooled or per-fold held-out prediction scores |
| `select_cv()` | Evaluate model selection using training-only AIC, AICc or BIC |

# Keep dependent observations together

Use the animal, site or other sampling unit that should not occur on both sides
of a split. This small example has two observations per sampling group.

```{r grouped-folds}
ids <- paste0("record", seq_len(12))
sampling_group <- rep(letters[1:6], each = 2)
grouped <- grouped_cv_folds(sampling_group, k = 3, ids = ids)
grouped
grouped$fold1
```

Each group belongs to one assessment fold; the other groups form the analysis
set. Assignment balances row counts using whole groups, largest first. It is
deterministic and does not alter the random-number generator. If random folds
are needed, supply a predeclared explicit list of analysis/assessment IDs to the
CV functions. They also accept repeated assessment splits and training-buffer
exclusions. Both vectors must be nonempty, disjoint character IDs within a split.

The GLM scoring adapters support Gaussian, Poisson, binomial, NB2 and Gamma
targets. Complete matched choice sets use the separate conditional-choice
adapter described below. Mixed, GAM, unmarked and Bayesian scoring require
their own qualified predictive targets and adapters.

# Use projected spatial blocks and a training buffer

The bundled count example has 100 sampling locations. Assign stable row IDs to
both the response data and the point object. The bundled locations are an
unreferenced simulated grid. For this example, define its Cartesian distances
in meters with an explicit local CRS. This is not a claim about real geographic
locations. Real data need their actual projected CRS, with an explicit transform
when necessary; never relabel longitude/latitude as linear coordinates. No
full-data centering or scaling is performed below.

```{r spatial-folds}
data("landscape_counts")
data("surv_pts")
dat <- landscape_counts
locations <- surv_pts
stopifnot(is.na(sf::st_crs(locations)))
local_crs <- paste0('LOCAL_CS["Simulated metre grid",LOCAL_DATUM["Local",0],',
                    'UNIT["metre",1],AXIS["X",EAST],AXIS["Y",NORTH]]')
sf::st_crs(locations) <- local_crs
ids <- paste0("site", seq_len(nrow(dat)))
rownames(dat) <- rownames(locations) <- ids
xy <- sf::st_coordinates(locations)
dat$east <- xy[, 1]

# Distances use the projected CRS units. Inspect them before choosing distances.
sf::st_crs(locations)$units_gdal
folds <- spatial_cv_folds(locations, block_size = 1000, k = 3, buffer = 100)
folds
```

An assessment fold can contain several disjoint blocks. The generator balances
counts; it does not create contiguous regions. With a positive buffer, the
training set excludes an entire spatial unit if any point in that unit lies
within the requested distance of an assessment point. The buffer measures
point-to-point separation, not distance to whole block boundaries.

Inspect `attr(folds, "fold_info")$assignment` for row, block, unit and fold
assignments and `$excluded` for training IDs removed per fold. For repeated
sampling, pass `group = dat$animal` or another aligned group vector. Blocks
connected by a shared group are joined, including transitive connections. If
too few units remain for `k` folds, or buffering removes every training unit,
the generator stops before model fitting. Coordinate tables require an explicit
projected `crs`; geographic coordinates are rejected rather than interpreted as
linear distances.

# Compare predictions from the same assessment targets

Start with inexpensive reference models. The trend below uses native `poly()`
metadata learned from each training set. The null model uses the same rows,
folds and Poisson observation definition.

```{r reference-models}
candidates <- list(
  null = cross_validate_glm(counts ~ 1, dat, folds, family = "poisson",
                            keep_selection = TRUE),
  trend = cross_validate_glm(counts ~ poly(east, 2), dat, folds, family = "poisson",
                             keep_selection = TRUE)
)
vapply(candidates, function(x) x$complete, logical(1))
cv_tab(candidates, metric = "neg_log_score")
cv_tab(candidates, metric = "rmse", by_fold = TRUE)
```

Lower scores are better. Negative log scores retain the Poisson count
probability, including its constants. RMSE is the square root of pooled squared
errors across assessment occurrences, not the average of fold RMSEs. If an
observation is assessed repeatedly, every occurrence contributes to the pooled
score. Frequency weights retain their replication meaning.

Binomial input can be numeric/logical 0/1, a two-level factor, or
`cbind(successes, failures)`. Binomial negative log scores compare count
probabilities; Brier scores average squared error over individual trials and
weight observations by frequency times trial count. A zero-trial row contributes
no score. An observed event assigned zero probability produces an infinite log
loss, which is retained without clipping.

`cv_tab()` requires matching analysis and assessment IDs, observed responses,
trials and frequency weights. It rejects incomplete candidates rather than
dropping failed folds. Inspect `$errors`, `$warnings` and `$diagnostics` before
interpreting scores. Completion means the requested calculations finished, not
that numerical diagnostics or calibration passed. Scores add no complexity
penalty and are not AIC values, Akaike weights or model probabilities. Variation
across dependent folds is not an independent-observation standard error.

# Validate overdispersed counts and positive responses

NB2 models allow count variance to exceed the mean. Their variance is
`mu + mu^2/theta`, where `mu` is the expected count and smaller `theta` means
greater extra variation. Gamma models describe strictly positive continuous
responses, with variance `dispersion * mu^2`. Both adapters use log links, so
`exp(coefficient)` is the multiplicative mean change for a one-unit predictor
change, conditional on the other model terms.

This deterministic example illustrates count-distribution comparison without
adding a spatial optimization or a simulation study.

```{r nb-reference-cv}
if (requireNamespace("MASS", quietly = TRUE)) {
  i <- 1:96
  count_dat <- data.frame(
    y = rep(c(0, 1, 0, 2, 9, 0, 1, 5, 0, 2, 14, 1), 8),
    x = sin(i * .73), group = factor(rep(letters[1:3], 32))
  )
  count_folds <- grouped_cv_folds(rep(letters[1:12], each = 8), k = 3)
  common_scores <- c("rmse", "mae", "neg_log_score")
  count_models <- list(
    poisson = cross_validate_glm(y ~ x + group, count_dat, count_folds,
      family = "poisson", metrics = common_scores, keep_selection = TRUE),
    nb = cross_validate_glm(y ~ x + group, count_dat, count_folds,
      family = "nbinom2", metrics = common_scores, keep_selection = TRUE)
  )
  cv_tab(count_models, metric = "neg_log_score")
  count_selected <- select_cv(count_models, criterion = "AIC", ties = "first")
  count_selected$selection$chosen
  lapply(count_selected$settings$fold_settings, `[[`, "family")
}
```

**How to read these results:** NB2 and Poisson log scores use the same observed
integer counts and retain every probability constant. Their ranking compares
the complete count distributions, including the NB2 theta estimated within
each training fold. Training AIC counts estimated theta once, together with
the native regression rank and any estimated ecological scales/shapes. A theta
fixed before CV adds no nuisance parameter. Each selected fold keeps its actual
family and nuisance metadata, so a Poisson winner has no invented NB2 theta.
Native convergence or theta-estimation warnings retain failed folds; do not
drop them to obtain a ranking. The exact Poisson limit follows the original
`joint_nb2` boundary gate and flag, rather than replacing theta with a large
finite number.
Joint-NB2 initializes coefficients with a native fixed-size GLM at `theta = 1`,
then estimates dispersion with the existing joint engine and its boundary
checks. This avoids requiring finite-theta alternation before the exact boundary
can be assessed. The initializer's size is neither a fixed fitted theta nor a prior.

Gamma CV freezes a different nuisance parameter. The next example uses positive
responses and a log-link Gamma mean.

```{r gamma-reference-cv}
i <- 1:96
positive_dat <- data.frame(
  y = exp(.2 + .35 * sin(i * .73)) * rep(c(.3, .6, 1.1, 2.4, .8, 1.8, .4, 1.6), 12),
  x = sin(i * .73)
)
positive_folds <- grouped_cv_folds(rep(letters[1:12], each = 8), k = 3)
gamma_cv <- cross_validate_glm(y ~ x, positive_dat, positive_folds,
                              family = "Gamma", keep_selection = TRUE)
gamma_cv$summary
lapply(gamma_cv$distribution, function(x) x[c("dispersion", "estimated", "convention")])
```

**How to read these results:** `dispersion` is the training deviance divided by
the training sum of case frequencies, matching native Gamma AIC. It is frozen
for held-out Gamma densities. Native coefficient SEs use their original Pearson
dispersion convention and can therefore use a different number. CV preserves
both roles; density dispersion does not replace coefficient uncertainty.

Use `theta = 3` or `dispersion = 0.4` only if that parameter is known or fixed
independently of assessment outcomes. Known Gamma dispersion uses its declared
normalized density from the start of fitting. Merely setting a native Gamma
family's dispersion field would change its parameter count while leaving its
AIC function's deviance estimate in place. The CV adapter avoids that mismatch
without changing global GLM methods or existing fitted objects.

Both families require integer nonnegative frequency weights. Native nobs is
the number of positive-weight training rows, not the sum of their frequencies.
Gamma outcomes must remain strictly positive and NB2 counts nonnegative
integers, including zero-weight rows. Their default scores are RMSE, MAE and
negative log score. Deviance is not offered as a comparison loss because its
saturated-density constants change with the nuisance parameter. RMSE/MAE can
compare compatible conditional means across families; density scores and
information criteria require the same continuous or discrete observation
measure. Gaussian density scoring is not qualified here.

For spatial fits, estimated NB2 supports `profile_glm`, `joint_nb2` and `refit`.
Gamma and fixed-theta NB2 require `refit`, which is selected when their backend
argument is omitted. Explicit incompatible choices stop before fitting.
Existing kernel/metric and numerical guards remain in force. Mean and supported
weighted-SQ predictors use the same frozen training normalization and reference
contract as the other GLMs.

```{r nb-gamma-spatial-cv, eval=FALSE}
# Use the same raw-cell inputs and predeclared folds as the other candidates.
nb_spatial <- cross_validate(counts ~ land1 + land2, dat, inputs, folds,
  family = "nbinom2", keep_selection = TRUE)
# For a separate positive-response data set, Gamma uses native refitting.
gamma_spatial <- cross_validate(positive ~ habitat + group, positive_observations,
  positive_inputs, positive_splits, family = "Gamma", backend = "refit",
  keep_selection = TRUE)
```

These scores condition on fitted mean and nuisance parameters. They integrate
neither parameter nor selection uncertainty, provide no observation intervals
and establish no calibration claim. Existing priors and diagnostics are unchanged.

# Evaluate a model-selection procedure within the folds

Per-fold assessment ranks describe prediction performance. They must not choose
the model whose predictions are then scored on those same observations.
`select_cv()` instead uses native **training likelihoods**, selecting by a
predeclared AIC, AICc or BIC rule and then retrieving the chosen model's held-out
predictions. No extra fitting is needed.

```{r training-selection}
selected <- select_cv(candidates, criterion = "AICc", ties = "first")
selected$selection$chosen
selected$selection$tables$fold1
cv_tab(c(candidates, list(training_selected = selected)), metric = "neg_log_score")
```

The native training tables retain their original parameter counts. Estimated
scales and shapes enter the existing multiScaleR penalty; fixed radii remain
fixed. Native nuisance parameters and likelihood-comparability guards are
unchanged. This example predeclares that exact criterion ties use the first
listed model. The default `ties = "error"` retains an unresolved tie as a failed
selection fold. Invalid or nonfinite training criteria are also retained as
failures, leaving the procedure's pooled scores incomplete.

The resulting score assesses this candidate set and selection rule. If pooled
CV results are used to choose the candidate set, kernel, block size or selection
rule itself, assess that final choice with an independent test set or a further
outer validation layer. Neither `cv_tab()` nor `select_cv()` integrates parameter
or selection uncertainty, supplies observation intervals or establishes
calibration.

# Add a model that estimates ecological scales

Reuse the same explicit folds with raw-cell preparation. This workflow is not
run during vignette builds because it adds a scale optimization for every fold.
The test suite checks training-only scale refitting and score agreement with
native GLMs. Choose the extraction domain and initial scales independently of
assessment outcomes.

```{r estimated-scales, eval=FALSE}
land <- terra::rast(system.file("extdata", "landscape.tif", package = "multiScaleR"))
# The example raster uses the same simulated grid and local distance declaration.
terra::crs(land) <- sf::st_crs(locations)$wkt
inputs <- kernel_prep(pts = locations, raster_stack = land,
                      max_D = 1500, sigma = c(250, 500, 250),
                      store_cell_data = TRUE)
# Prepared and response rows must have exactly the same IDs and order.
stopifnot(identical(rownames(inputs$kernel_dat), rownames(dat)))
spatial <- cross_validate(counts ~ land1 + land2, dat, inputs, folds,
                          family = "poisson", keep_selection = TRUE)
models <- c(candidates, list(spatial = spatial))
cv_tab(models, metric = "neg_log_score")
selection <- select_cv(models, criterion = "AICc", ties = "first")
```

`cross_validate()` rebuilds spatial predictors inside every training set,
estimates scales and coefficients there, and freezes its learned normalization
and bin references for assessment prediction. It preserves existing starts,
cold/limiting/curvature checks and metric/kernel guards. Do not supply full-data
scale fits as substitutes for fold fits. Ordinary reference models use
`cross_validate_glm()`; the spatial entry point still requires an optimized
spatial predictor. Grouped fold generation is distinct from grouped raster
preparation. The former defines sampling units for validation; the latter
chooses a fixed covariate map for each row.

## Use fixed maps for different raster groups

Modern `kernel_prep_by_group()` inputs retain raw buffers and a named
`raster_group` mapping. CV validates this mapping before fitting, subsets it
with the buffers and records analysis/assessment assignments in `$raster_groups`.
Training normalization and bin references still use training rows only.

```{r grouped-raster-cv, eval=FALSE}
# Both labels use the same simulated map here solely to illustrate alignment.
# For real data, supply the appropriate maps with identical grids and layer names.
maps <- list(map1 = land, map2 = land)
map_id <- rep(c("map1", "map2"), length.out = nrow(locations))
group_inputs <- kernel_prep_by_group(locations, maps, group = map_id,
                                    max_D = 1500, store_cell_data = TRUE)
grouped_cv <- cross_validate(counts ~ land1 + land2, dat, group_inputs, folds,
                             family = "poisson")
grouped_cv$raster_groups$fold1
```

Raster-map labels do not themselves introduce annual random effects, varying
scales or extra fitted parameters. Explicit formula factors/interactions and
estimated scales/shapes keep their native parameter penalties. A held-out factor
level absent from training still produces the native prediction failure; CV does
not replace it with a zero effect. Inspect the selected row/map records and
`$selection$candidate_settings` when evaluating a training-selection procedure.
`$settings$controls_from` identifies the first candidate whose control fields
are inherited; candidate-specific controls remain in the selection record.

## Retain cells intersecting the extraction buffer

Native raster preparation records both cell dimensions. A cell can intersect
the extraction buffer even when its center lies beyond the nominal radius.
CV retains those values and fixes the bin domain using the requested radius
plus half the pixel diagonal, rather than a maximum learned from held-out rows.
Representative distances and normalization are still learned only from training
rows. Geometry is frozen with the bin reference. Legacy saved inputs without
cell geometry keep the original strict gate; prepare them again with the current
constructor if that gate rejects their cell-center distances. Extraction,
kernel/metric definitions and fitted parameter bounds are unchanged.

# Validate step selection within complete choice sets

A step-selection model predicts which alternative is used within a defined
choice set. Those probabilities differ from independent Bernoulli occurrence
probabilities and from unnormalized relative selection scores. Use
`cross_validate_clogit()` for one used alternative and at least one available
alternative per set. Keep all alternatives together in every split.

The following deterministic example illustrates the software workflow. It is
not a movement-data study or an assessment of animal-level transfer.

```{r conditional-choice-cv}
if (requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE)) {
  i <- 1:72
  set <- (i - 1L) %/% 3L
  choices <- data.frame(
    used = as.numeric((i - 1L) %% 3L == set %% 3L),
    step = set + 1L, habitat = sin(i * 1.7), effort = 1 + (i %% 4) / 10
  )
  # Hold out entire choice sets, including the used and available alternatives.
  choice_folds <- grouped_cv_folds(choices$step, k = 3)
  choice_models <- list(
    null = cross_validate_clogit(used ~ strata(step), choices, choice_folds,
                                 keep_selection = TRUE),
    habitat = cross_validate_clogit(
      used ~ habitat + offset(log(effort)) + strata(step),
      choices, choice_folds, keep_selection = TRUE
    )
  )
  cv_tab(choice_models, metric = "neg_log_score")
  choice_selection <- select_cv(choice_models, criterion = "AICc", ties = "first")
  choice_selection$selection$chosen
  choice_selection$selection$tables$fold1
  choice_selection$summary
}
```

**How to read these results:** Each loss is the negative natural logarithm of
the used alternative's probability among its complete set. Lower scores are
better. The average and assessment counts refer to choice sets; every alternative
remains in `$predictions`, and `$summary$n_alternatives` reports their count.
Log scores are calculated in log space, so a tiny displayed probability that
rounds to zero does not create a false infinite loss. Losses that exceed the
numeric range remain infinite and are never clipped.

The null model has no estimated response coefficients. CV validates survival's
stored scalar null likelihood against the complete-set offset likelihood before
using it for training selection. Missing or inconsistent metadata remains a
failure. Other native Cox objects and methods are unchanged. The native training
table uses one event per analysis set for AICc/BIC and counts all estimated
response coefficients and ecological scale/shape parameters. It does not use
the number of available alternatives as the event count.

The example validates transfer to other choice sets under this split plan. For
transfer to new animals, construct folds from the animal IDs instead. If step
labels repeat across animals, first create a globally unique choice ID, such as
`interaction(animal, step, drop = TRUE)`, and use that column in `strata()`.
For spatial blocks, supply choice IDs or whole-animal IDs as the grouping
constraint so alternatives cannot cross split boundaries. The CV validator
rejects incomplete sets before any fitting.

To estimate ecological scales within those same folds, supply raw-cell
`kernel_inputs` and choose `backend = "conditional_logit"` or `"refit"`.
Existing kernel/metric admission, independent starts, cold/native checks and
curvature rules remain. Initial and fitted normalization and representative
bin distances use analysis rows only. Assessment predictors use those frozen
references, including when their distances enter different training bins.
Prepared raster-map groups remain fixed covariate inputs and add no annual or
random effects by themselves.

Fixed factors, interactions, offsets and supported saved polynomial/spline
terms use native training metadata. Dot formulas expand declared column names
without learning assessment transformations. Exclude the set ID as an ordinary
predictor, for example `used ~ . - step + strata(step)`; coefficients for
predictors constant within every set are not identified. Retain native alias
and convergence failures instead of silently dropping terms or alternatives.

Use the same declared exact, Efron or Breslow method across candidates. This
adapter accepts unweighted, unpenalized one-case sets. Robust clustering,
frailty/special Cox terms and generic censored survival prediction need their
own scoring targets. `cv_tab()` keeps conditional choice separate from GLM
scores. As with the GLM workflow, inspect original diagnostics, retain failures
and use outer assessment if these results tune the candidate set or selection
rule. These point scores integrate no parameter/selection uncertainty and
provide no observation intervals or calibration certificate.

# Keep outputs proportionate to the task

Both CV functions default to `keep_fits = FALSE` and `keep_selection = FALSE`,
retaining scores, training summaries and diagnostics. For training-based model
selection, use `keep_selection = TRUE`. Each `$selection_records` entry captures
the actual training fit's native log likelihood, full parameter count, effective
likelihood rows, outcomes/trials/frequencies, formula text, controls and original
diagnostics. It stores no fitted model, design matrix, raw raster or formula
environment. Records are smaller than full fits, but their row metadata still
grows with the number of observations and folds.

`select_cv()` checks those records against the split and target identities and
uses the same likelihood-comparability guards and criterion table constructors.
If you retain both records and full fits, they must agree exactly. A metadata
failure is retained as a selection failure and does not erase a candidate's
otherwise valid held-out predictions. Records do not change diagnostic eligibility.

Use `keep_fits = TRUE` when you need to inspect native fits or return selected
fits with `select_cv(..., keep_fits = TRUE)`. Records cannot reconstruct full
models. Older CV results with retained fits still work; older score-only results
need a new run with `keep_selection = TRUE` before training-based selection.
`select_cv()` returns compact output by default. Reuse the
same prepared inputs and fold list across candidates, and avoid saving duplicate
rasters or arrays of fit objects as intermediate checkpoints.

For inference-target and interval distinctions, see
`vignette("inference-contracts", package = "multiScaleR")`. For likelihood-based
model comparison, see `?aic_tab` and `?bic_tab`. Function help for `?cross_validate`,
`?spatial_cv_folds`, `?cv_tab` and `?select_cv` gives the complete input and
result contracts.
